title: Why We Resist Demand and Commands
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article explains "psychological reactance," the well-documented tendency for people to push back against anything that restricts their sense of free choice, and applies it directly to leadership communication. It argues that outright demands and commands reliably trigger internal or overt resistance, while suggestions, recommendations, and invitations produce far less friction while still achieving compliance. The piece also notes that some leaders and parents exploit reactance deliberately through reverse psychology, though it cautions this tactic can backfire and should be used sparingly.
points: Psychological reactance describes the automatic urge to resist anything that restricts one's sense of free choice.
Demands and commands from leaders reliably trigger this resistance, even when unspoken.
Suggestions, recommendations, and invitations achieve compliance with far less friction than direct orders.
Reverse psychology exploits reactance deliberately but can backfire and should be used cautiously.
Leaders who understand reactance can avoid unintentionally provoking resistance through the way they phrase requests.
quotes: It’s amazing how powerful the need is to resist any restriction of our personal freedoms.
When confronted by a demand or a command that curtails their freedom, people are motivated to restore their autonomy through a process called “psychological reactance.
Any time a leader makes a demand or commands what team members must do, they set off this psychological reactance.
Good leaders quickly learn that direction, instruction, suggestion, and recommendation produce far less noise and resistance than demand, command, and control.
Understanding the human motivation to react to anyone or anything that restricts our freedom is a central tenet of sound leadership.
